stem: Two weeks ago your team rewrote the tool descriptions. `process_refund` now says it issues a new refund and is not for checking refund status. `lookup_order` now says it returns order details including refund status. Misrouting persists: in 9% of conversations where a customer asks about an existing refund (e.g., "where's my refund for #5521?"), the agent calls `process_refund`. The backend rejects these as duplicates, so no money moves, but most of these conversations end in escalation. Logs show 96% of the misrouted calls come from messages containing the word "refund". The same status question phrased as "where's my money for #5521?" routes correctly to `lookup_order`. The system prompt contains: "Whenever a customer mentions a refund, use process_refund to resolve it promptly." What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Rewrite the system-prompt line so `process_refund` is tied to a request for a new refund rather than to the word "refund", letting the descriptions govern selection.
options.B: Add three few-shot examples to the system prompt showing refund-status questions routed to `lookup_order`, keeping the existing refund instruction as written.
options.C: Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks `process_refund` when the order already has a refund on file and returns an error pointing the agent to `lookup_order`.
options.D: Consolidate `lookup_order` and `process_refund` into one `manage_order` tool with an `action` parameter so a single description covers both operations.

stem: Your team split the support agent into a coordinator and three specialist agents (billing-dispute, returns, account). To cut latency, an engineer changed the flow so the billing-dispute agent passes its findings straight to the returns agent through a shared queue instead of reporting back. Since then, in 7% of tickets that combine a billing dispute with a return, the billing lookup times out. The returns agent then issues a refund from partial data, and the coordinator marks the ticket resolved. Coordinator traces contain no record of the timeout. Which change most effectively fixes this?

options.A: Have the returns agent re-run the billing lookup itself whenever a queued handoff arrives incomplete, before it calls process_refund.
options.B: Route every handoff between specialist agents back through the coordinator, so it sees each result or error and picks the next step.
options.C: Add structured error fields to the shared-queue payload so the returns agent sees the billing agent's timeout and partial results.
options.D: Add a SubagentStop hook that writes each queued handoff into the coordinator's trace log so the timeout is recorded there.

stem: Your agent's system prompt contains a detailed returns and billing policy and five few-shot examples, all clear-cut cases such as an in-window return with photos or an obvious duplicate charge. A review of 300 recent tickets shows that clear-cut cases get the same action 96% of the time. Two borderline patterns behave differently: damage reported 3–10 days past the return window, and partial-charge disputes where the customer's account conflicts with the order record. Near-identical tickets in these patterns get refunds, escalations, and denials in roughly equal shares. In those transcripts, the agent quotes the correct policy clause before choosing an action. All of these tickets are under $150, a PreToolUse hook already blocks `process_refund` above $500, and the policy team says most of these cases should be resolved without a human. Which change will most effectively make the agent handle these two patterns consistently?

options.A: Add 12–15 more few-shot examples sampled at random from last quarter's resolved tickets so the agent sees a wider range of real support cases.
options.B: Add a PreToolUse hook that intercepts `process_refund` on these two ticket patterns and redirects them to `escalate_to_human` for a decision.
options.C: Move the policy clauses for these two patterns to the top of the system prompt under explicit section headers so they are not lost in the middle.
options.D: Replace two of the existing examples with three worked examples of these ticket patterns, each showing the chosen action and why the others were rejected.

stem: Billing-dispute conversations with your agent often run past 40 turns. stem: An audit of 400 transcripts that involved a handoff decision finds two patterns. In 31 of them, the customer asked to talk to a person, worded in many different ways ("is anyone real there?", "get me your manager", "I'm done with the bot"). The agent kept troubleshooting for three to five more turns before calling `escalate_to_human`, following a system-prompt line that says to attempt resolution first. In 58 others, the customer used angry language about a late-delivery refund that the policy covers but never asked for a person, and the agent handed off on the first turn without offering the refund. Handoff volume rose 20% after a recent edit added "escalate when the customer seems upset." Which change most effectively corrects both patterns?

options.A: Add a pre-call hook that scans each message for terms like "human," "manager," or "person" and calls `escalate_to_human` before the model replies, keeping rules for covered refunds as is.
options.B: Replace the "seems upset" line with a separate model that scores sentiment on each customer turn, and hand off only when anger stays above a tuned threshold for two turns.
options.C: Have the agent rate its confidence in resolving each case from 1 to 10, escalate immediately below 6, and add few-shot examples of offer-versus-escalation calls.
options.D: Rewrite the escalation rules: honor a request for a person immediately; for anger over a covered issue, offer the fix and hand off only if the customer still insists; add few-shot examples.

stem: During a 40-minute order-database failover last week, the `lookup_order` MCP server's timeout handler retried each call three times with exponential backoff (about 20 seconds in total). It then returned `{"orders": []}` with `isError: false`. The agent told 312 customers that no order matched their number and asked them to re-check it. 41% contacted support again the same day, and transcripts show frustration rising. On normal days, about 6% of lookups correctly return no match because the customer reads out a cart or quote number instead of an order number. The agent handles those cases well by asking for the email address on the order. The `lookup_order` description was rewritten last month, and tool-selection accuracy is now above 98%. Which change would most effectively prevent this from happening again?

options.A: Add a system-prompt rule telling the agent to retry `lookup_order` once on an empty result and then call `escalate_to_human` if the list is still empty.
options.B: Have the server return `isError: true` on timeouts, with a transient `errorCategory`, `isRetryable: true`, and a note that the order system was unreachable.
options.C: Raise the server's timeout retry limit from three to ten attempts with a longer backoff ceiling before it returns the empty order list.
options.D: Add a `PostToolUse` hook that marks every empty `lookup_order` result as `isError: true` so the agent stops telling customers an order doesn't exist.

stem: No one has edited the four tool descriptions in five months. The `escalate_to_human` description is two sentences long and does not mention billing. Eight days ago, compliance appended a section to the system prompt stating that disputes require human-verified account history. Compliance has since confirmed that the requirement covers only chargebacks filed with the card issuer. Since the change, the agent has called `escalate_to_human` on 27% of billing conversations, up from 4%, and first-contact resolution has dropped 9 points. Reviewers sampled 200 of those escalations. In 91% of them, the customer was asking whether a credit for a disputed charge had posted, which `lookup_order` answers, and the agent's text often cited verification before it escalated. Which change most effectively restores correct tool selection?

options.A: Expand the `escalate_to_human` tool description with billing boundaries stating that disputed-charge status questions belong to `lookup_order`.
options.B: Add a pre-call hook that blocks `escalate_to_human` on dispute conversations unless a chargeback was filed with the card issuer.
options.C: Reword the new system-prompt section so it is limited to issuer chargebacks and names the tool for other disputes.
options.D: Add a few-shot section to the system prompt showing credit-status questions on disputed charges resolved through `lookup_order`.

stem: Your support coordinator sends every ticket through four subagents (identity verification, order history, billing analysis, returns eligibility) and merges their outputs into one reply. A two-week trace review found that 58% of tickets are single-issue order-status questions, and every trace shows all four subagents invoked. On those order-status tickets, the billing analysis subagent labeled routine pending authorizations as a "possible duplicate charge" 9% of the time. The coordinator relayed these notes to customers, which generated new billing contacts. The billing team also reviewed the same subagent's output on tickets where customers disputed a charge and found it accurate. They want pending authorizations surfaced on those tickets, because real duplicates often show up first as pending authorizations. About one ticket in six combines an order question with a charge question. Median handling time is 41 seconds against a 90-second target. An engineer proposes running the three post-verification subagents concurrently, since each depends only on the verified customer ID. Verification must still precede any order or refund operation. Which change most effectively addresses the review's findings?

options.A: Issue the three post-verification subagent calls together in one coordinator turn so they run concurrently, since each needs only the verified customer ID.
options.B: Add a PostToolUse hook that drops the billing subagent's findings before the merge whenever the ticket has been tagged as an order-status inquiry.
options.C: Rewrite the billing subagent's prompt with explicit criteria so it flags a duplicate only when two settled charges match on amount, merchant, and date.
options.D: Keep verification as the fixed first step, then have the coordinator decide per ticket which of the other specialists the customer's request needs.
